Birds and Vegetation of Shade Coffee Plantations in Chikmagalur, Central Western Ghats, India

Overview: This dataset contains bird community and vegetation data collected from 12 shade coffee plantation estates and two sites within Bhadra Tiger Reserve in the Chikmagalur District of Karnataka, India, between December 2005 and May 2006. The data were collected as part of an MSc thesis at the National Centre for Biological Sciences and the Centre for Wildlife Studies. The study examines how local-scale habitat properties and landscape-scale factors (viz. distance to contiguous forests) influence bird species richness and abundance in shade coffee plantations of the Western Ghats biodiversity hotspot.

birds and vegetation of shade coffee plantations in chikmagalur, central western ghats, india

overview: this dataset contains bird community and vegetation data collected from 12 shade coffee plantation estates and two sites within bhadra tiger reserve in the chikmagalur district of karnataka, india, between december 2005 and may 2006. the data were collected as part of an msc thesis at the national centre for biological sciences and the centre for wildlife studies. the study examines how local-scale habitat properties and landscape-scale factors (viz. distance to contiguous forests) influence bird species richness and abundance in shade coffee plantations of the western ghats biodiversity hotspot.

associated publication: anand, m. o., krishnaswamy, j., and das, a. (2008). proximity to forests drives bird conservation value of coffee plantations: implications for certification. ecological applications, 18(7), 1754–1763. https://doi.org/10.1890/07-1839.1

study site: the fieldwork was conducted in the foothills of the bababudan hills, chikmagalur district, karnataka, india. coffee (arabica and robusta varieties) plantations in the district cover over 870 km² and contribute close to 25% of all coffee produced from the western ghats. plantations are almost entirely grown under a shade layer, which ranges from native shade trees to monocultures of the introduced species, silver oak (grevillea robusta). this study was carried out within 12 private coffee estates and two sites within muthodi forests of bhadra tiger reserve. birds were sampled using point-counts and saturation was verified using variable-length transects of 50 birds. vegetation (trees) were sampled either using 10m radius plots or point-centered quarters, and structure and composition of vegetation was measured within these plots.

bird sampling -- point counts: at each of the 14 sites, birds were sampled in 5-minute variable radius (max: 70m) point counts between 06:50 and 09:30 am. all birds (excluding soaring raptors, swifts, and swallows) seen or heard were recorded at the highest possible taxonomic level, their abundances noted, and their distance measured using a laser rangefinder. each site had a median of 10 point-count locations (min: 9, max: 12), sampled four times: two seasons, and two rounds of sampling in each season. additional information such as microhabitat of the bird and the strata in which it was detected, were also recorded.

bird sampling -- point counts (metadata): metadata of each point count were also recorded. these were: geographic coordinates, date and time of sampling, dominant canopy type, number of mature trees at the point count station, the proportion of silver oak in the canopy, and a score of the leaf litter. vegetation variables came from additional vegetation sampling (more details below).

Title: Mammal occurrence records (2025-26) in central and southern Western Ghats, India

Description:

This dataset contains mammal occurrence records (June 2025 - February 2026) from the Western Ghats, collected using a mobile collection application (EpiCollect5).

Suggested citation is:
Nature Conservation Foundation (2026). Mammal occurrence records (2025-26) in the Valparai Plateau and Anamalai Tiger Reserve, Western Ghats, India. Nature Conservation Foundation, India. Dataset, Zenodo. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.18923778

This includes data from the project, Western Ghats Mammals
(https://five.epicollect.net/project/western-ghats-mammals (PRIVATE project), 1st June 2025 - 28th February 2026, n=1943)

This dataset follows from a previous upload of records from the Western Ghats Mammals Project (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.18910401)


Dataset contacts and Project leaders:
Name: T. R. Shankar Raman
Institution: Nature Conservation Foundation, India
Email: trsr@ncf-india.org
ORCID: 0000-0002-1347-3953

Name: Divya Mudappa
Institution: Nature Conservation Foundation, India
Email: divya@ncf-india.org
ORCID: 0000-0001-9708-4826
    
Keywords: tropical rainforests, plantations, Anamalai Hills, Western Ghats, animal distribution, mammals

Geographic Coverage:
1. Location/Study Area: Multiple locations along the Western Ghats, India; Anamalai Tiger Reserve, Tamil Nadu, India
2. GPS coordinates: 
All records: 73.80242° - 77.59048° and  10.25200° - 17.93301°
Main locations: Sakleshpur region, Nilgiris, Valparai Plateau and Anamalai Tiger Reserve

Temporal Coverage:
1. Begins: 2025-06-01 (Year, Month, Day)
2. Ends: 2026-02-28 (Year, Month, Day)

Besides the 00_readMe.txt file containing this information, the dataset includes 77 images (photographs) and 2 comma-delimited text (csv) files and one R-script as explained below:

1. 01_epicollect4zenodo.csv
eventID - Unique event ID
occurrenceID - Unique occurrence ID for each observation
institutionID - Institution ID
institutionCode - Institution Code
eventDate - Date of observation in YYYY-MM-DD format
eventTime - Time of observation in hh:mm:ss + 05:30 UTC (for IST zone)
decimalLatitude - Latitude in decimal degrees N
decimalLongitude - Longitude in decimal degrees N
coordinateUncertaintyInMeters - Horizontal accuracy of GPS location in metres or estimated accuracy
recordedBy - Name of observer
associatedMedia - If available, filenames of associated photographs (.jpg)
verbatimIdentification - Identification common name as recorded on the EpiCollect form
scientificName - Scientific name of the species as matched to GBIF backbone

02_namesMatch.csv
commonName - Identification common name as recorded on the EpiCollect form
sciName - Scientific name of the species as matched to GBIF backbone
# Note: Other category used for other species marked as NA

03_epicollect4gbif_Rscript_for_reference.R
R code used for porting the data to Darwin Core format for upload to GBIF

DATA & CODE FILE OVERVIEW
This data repository consists of three .csv files, one code script and this metadata document. The raw data files for ungulates, snow leopards and livestock have not been uploaded due to safety concerns to avoid misuse (poaching) and can be provided upon request. The data files provided include density estimates of each.

sl_densityestimate.csv


ungulate_densityestimate.csv - Contains density and abundance estimates of wild ungulates (blue sheep and ibex) estimated using the double observer survey.
Variable names and descriptions:
year - year of sampling
Pop.estimate - abundance estimate of wild ungulates
Lower.95.CI - lower 95% confidence interval of abundance estimate
Upper.95.CI - upper 95% confidence interval of abundance estimate
Est.groups - estimated number of ungulate groups/herds
Mean.group.size - mean group size of ungulate herds
Detection.obs1 - detection probability of observer 1
Detection.obs2 - detection probability of observer 2
ung_den - wild ungulate density (abundance divided by study area, i.e. 725)
ung_lcl - lower 95% confidence interval of wild ungulate density (lcl of abundance divided by study area, i.e. 725)
ung_ucl - upper 95% confidence interval of wild ungulate density (ucl of abundance divided by study area, i.e. 725)

livestock_count_dep.csv - Contains livestock population count and depredation by snow leopards collected through census via key-informant surveys.

year - year of sampling

livestock_dep - number of all livestock depredated by snow leopards

lambda0_ucl - upper 95% confidence interval of cumulative hazard of detection estimate
sigma - sigma (movement) estimate

title: Data from: Deciduous forests hold conservation value for birds within South Andaman Island, India
codebook:
[ReadMe.txt]
Data from: Deciduous forests hold conservation value for birds within South Andaman Island, India

Authors:- Arpitha Jayanth (1,2,*), Zankhna Patel (1), Mohammed Mubeen (1), Karthikayan M (3), Rohit Naniwadekar (1)

Affiliations:-
(1) Nature Conservation Foundation, 1311, “Amritha”, 12th Main, Vijayanagar 1st Stage, Mysuru 570 017, Karnataka, India
(2) National Centre for Biological Sciences, Tata Institute of Fundamental Research, Bengaluru 560 065, Karnataka, India
(3) Department of Ecology and Environmental Sciences, Pondicherry University, Pondicherry, 605 014, India

Corresponding author:- *Arpitha Jayanth (arpitha.jayanth@gmail.com)

****************************************************************

We assessed the importance of deciduous and evergreen habitats for forest birds (including several endemic and threatened species) within South Andaman Island.
To this end, we compared the composition and diversity (taxonomic, functional and phylogenetic) of forest birds across the two habitat types, and evaluated species-specific responses to habitat variables within the island.
The dataset collected and R codes used for this study are published here. Bird species traits were sourced from Tobias et al. (2022) and Wilman et al. (2014). Phylogenetic trees were sourced from birdtree.org (Jetz et al. 2012).

Geographic Coverage: South Andaman Island, Andaman and Nicobar Islands, India
Taxonomic Coverage: Birds, 54 species
Temporal Coverage: March-May 2022 and December 2022-April 2023

****************************************************************

Brief summary of field methods:- 

We conducted line-transect surveys for forest birds across evergreen and deciduous forests in South Andaman Island, India. 
Twenty-seven transects were sampled either in the morning (between 0515 – 0930 hrs) or in the afternoon (between 1515 – 1730 hrs) from March-May 2022 and December 2022-April 2023.
For every bird detected, we noted species identity, group size (if visible), time of detection, and whether the bird(s) was seen or heard.
Detections of flying birds and nocturnal species (owls and nightjars) were excluded.
For each transect, we measured - 
a. tree density and basal area (using the point-centered quarter method, or PCQ); 
b. canopy cover, proportion of deciduous trees, and presence of cane, bamboo runners and clumps of standing bamboo (averaged across PCQ points);
c. number of large trees and cut logs (counted within a 20m-wide belt along each transect); and 
d. distance from nearest settlement/village (using Google Earth Pro).

****************************************************************

Description of data files:-

1. species_list.csv - This dataset contains all 54 bird species codes and scientific names used in the analysis
sp_id: four-letter bird species code, used consistently throughout the analysis
sp_latest: latest scientific name of bird species
sp_tree: scientific name used for extracting phylogenet

METHODS

Methods used for ecological restoration of degraded rainforest fragments following a mixed native species planting protocol (maximum diversity) are as described in Raman et al. (2009, Restoration Ecology 17:137–147. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1526-100X.2008.00367.x ). 

Monitoring Protocol
All planted species were identified based on prior researchexperience and field guides (Gamble & Fischer 1915–1935; Pascal & Ramesh 1997). Each seedling was marked with biodegradable flagging tape and tagged with thin metal tags with eyelets fastened to seedlings by metal wire with the species code and plant number impressed on the metal tag with a pen. The seedlings were monitored for survival at 6-month intervals for the first 2 years: in December–January after the plants’ first wet season, in May–June after the first dry season, and likewise during the following year after the plants’ second wet and dry seasons. For two of the larger sites planted in 2004 (I1-04, S1-04), approximately 250 seedlings were randomly selected from among all planted areas. Data were collected regarding state (dead or alive), condition (browsed, cut, insect herbivory), and growth of each seedling. In addition, photographic documentation and standard quadrat sampling were conducted every 6 months and 2 years, respectively (results not presented here; Fig. 1).

title: Line transect data on birds from Mudumalai and Upper Nilgiris, India
codebook:
[00_README.txt]
This dataset contains data on bird communities from variable-width line transect surveys carried out in 1995-96 in the Mudumalai Wildlife Sanctuary (now Tiger Reserve) and Upper Nilgiris, Tamil Nadu, India. The data were collected on a project of the Centre for Ecological Sciences, Indian Institute of Science, Bangalore.

GEOGRAPHICAL AREA: Mudumalai Wildlife Sanctuary (now Tiger Reserve) and Upper Nilgiris, Tamil Nadu, India

TAXONOMIC SCOPE: Birds

ACKNOWLEDGEMENT: I am grateful to Dr R. Sukumar for the opportunity to survey these transects and to P. Pavithra and Palani for help with data.

METHODS

Bird data are from 1200 m long (0.75 miles) line transect surveys surveyed typically in about 100-120 min duration in the early morning hours. The methods for bird sampling are as described in Raman (2003) and in this doctoral thesis:
Raman, T. R. S. 2001. Community ecology and conservation of mid-elevation tropical rainforest bird communities in the southern Western Ghats, India. PhD thesis, Indian Institute of Science, Bangalore.

All transects were censused during the first 3 h after sunrise when bird activity was highest in the area walking at a slow, uniform pace. All birds seen (perched or flying under the canopy) or heard were recorded as to species, number (wherever possible) and perpendicular distance in the following metre classes: 0–5, 5–10, etcwith the further distance classes being wider to minimize errors in distance estimation.

USAGE NOTES

Besides this 00_README.txt file, this dataset contains the following 3 comma-delimited text files with data in columns as explained below.

01_niltrans.csv
This contains information on the line transects
date: date of survey in year-month-date format
transect: name of transect
stratum: habitat stratum
decimalLatitude: latitude in decimal degrees N
decimalLongitude: longitude in decimal degrees E
coordinateUncertaintyInMeters: approximate uncertainty in metres as exact location is unknown
duration: duration of survey in minutes
startTime: transect start time in the morning in hh:mm format
endTime: transect end time in the morning in hh:mm format
weather: notes on weather
remarks: other remarks

02_nilbirds.csv
This contains the transect bird data
date: date of survey in year-month-date format
transect: name of transect
startTime: transect start time in the morning in hh:mm format

heardSeenFlying: H - heard, s - Seen, F - Flying

title: The thermal niche and phylogenetic assembly of evergreen tree metacommunities in a mid-to-upper tropical montane zone
codebook:
[README.txt]
This dataset contains three data files and supplementary image of the phylogenetic tree used
in analysis.

The first data file called 'Dasetal2022_Nilgiris_spabundancebysite.csv' contains species
abundance data for each of the study plots.

The second data file called 'Dasetal2022_Nilgiris_focalsplist.csv' contains the data on study 
species which was used as input to create the phylogenetic tree in the R software
package 'v.phylomaker'. Empty cells are marked as 'NA'.

The third data file called 'Dasetal2022_Nilgiri_shola_env.csv' contains the data for
each of the microclimatic and macroclimatic predictors used in the analysis.
The columns in this file are as follows:

Column		Description
Plot.no	- Number of the 20x20m vegetation plot used to sample tree and shrub species > 1cm dbh
mean.diur.tmp.rng - Mean Diurnal Range (Mean of monthly (max temp - min temp)); (bio2 in BIOCLIM v.2 dataset, Fick and Hijmans 2017)
tmp.seas - Temperature Seasonality (standard deviation *100); (bio4 in BIOCLIM v2 dataset, Fick and Hijmans 2017)
max.tmp.warm - Max Temperature of Warmest Month; (bio5 in BIOCLIM v2 dataset, Fick and Hijmans 2017)
min.tmp.cold - Min Temperature of Coldest Month; (bio6 in BIOCLIM v2 dataset, Fick and Hijmans 2017)
prec.seas - Precipitation Seasonality (Coefficient of Variation); (bio15 in BIOCLIM v2 dataset, Fick and Hijmans 2017)
elevation - Elevation in mASL
elev.zone - zone 1: 1700-1999m; zone 2: 2000 - 2199m; zone 3: 2200 - 2500m
ln.area - ln of shola forest patch area
d.edge - distance from nearest shola forest edge in meters

title: Woody debris removal modifies carbon stocks and soil properties in a fragmented tropical rainforest
codebook:
[Nandakumar_et_al_metadata.txt]
The download includes a compressed folder that contains six CSV files whose contents are described below:
1) Nandakumar_et_al_CWD.csv
2) Nandakumar_et_al_CWD_density.csv
3) Nandakumar_et_al_CWD_vegetation.csv
4) Nandakumar_et_al_CWD_soil.csv
5) Nandakumar_et_al_CWD_soil_other.csv
6) Osuri_et_al_CWD.csv

-----File 1: "Nandakumar_et_al_CWD.csv"-----

Description: This file contains dimensions of all Coarse Woody Debris (CWD) with diameter above 10 cm, within 20m x 20m vegetation plots. For standing CWD and stumps from past logging, one diameter and height was measured. For fallen CWD, diameters at the two ends of the CWD where the diameter is atleast 10 cm, and the length between these diameters were measured. For CWD falling partially outside the plot, diameter at and length of CWD inside the plot boundary was measured. Each row represents one piece of CWD.

Column names and descriptions

id: Unique code assigned to an edge-interior vegetation plot pair
plot.remarks: General remarks about the plot and whether the plot is edge or interior plot.
class: Decay class of CWD. Criteria for deciding decay classes is given in the supplementary (Table S1)
state: Whether the CWD is on the ground, is standing or is the remaining stump of a logged tree
dia1: 1st diameter of the CWD (cm)
dia2: 2nd diameter of the CWD (cm). This will be absent for Standing CWD and stumps from past logging
cwd_group.pom: The point of measurement of the diameter, for standing CWD
height: Height/length of the CWD (m)
cwd_group.hole: Whether there was a cavity in the CWD
hole.depth: If there is a cavity, what is its depth (cm)
hole.dia: If there is a cavity, what is its diameter (cm)
cwd.remarks: General remarks about the CWD and shape of the cavity if present.
edg_int: Whether the plot is an edge or interior plot.
treatment: Whether its a plot near settlements (fuelwood_removal) or far away from settlements (control)

-----File 2: "Nandakumar_et_al_CWD_density.csv"-----

Description: This file contains the density of CWD of diameter greater than 10 cm in different decay classes. CWD were arbitrarily selected along different trails. Cores were extracted from CWD from each density class and water displacement method was used for estimating density.

Column names and description

Place: Site where the CWD was found
Status: Whether the CWD was fallen or standing. Wether the CWD was fully touching the soil (on-ground) or starting to slant is indicated in square brackets
Class: Decay class of the CWD
Code: Unique code assigned to the CWD
Volume 1-4: Volume of the cores extracted from the CWD (cm3). If there were more than one core from a single CWD, they are assigned in different columns
Mass: Mass of the cores after air-drying till constant weight (g).
Remarks.Condition: Remarks about the CWD and condition of the core.
dens: density of the core (g/m3), calculated using the formula volume/mass.

-----File 3: "Nandakumar_et_al_vegetation.csv"---
content:
woody debris removal modifies carbon stocks and soil properties in a fragmented tropical rainforest [nandakumar_et_al_metadata.txt]
the download includes a compressed folder that contains six csv files whose contents are described below:
1) nandakumar_et_al_cwd.csv
2) nandakumar_et_al_cwd_density.csv
3) nandakumar_et_al_cwd_vegetation.csv
4) nandakumar_et_al_cwd_soil.csv
5) nandakumar_et_al_cwd_soil_other.csv
6) osuri_et_al_cwd.csv

-----file 1: "nandakumar_et_al_cwd.csv"-----

description: this file contains dimensions of all coarse woody debris (cwd) with diameter above 10 cm, within 20m x 20m vegetation plots. for standing cwd and stumps from past logging, one diameter and height was measured. for fallen cwd, diameters at the two ends of the cwd where the diameter is atleast 10 cm, and the length between these diameters were measured. for cwd falling partially outside the plot, diameter at and length of cwd inside the plot boundary was measured. each row represents one piece of cwd.

column names and descriptions

id: unique code assigned to an edge-interior vegetation plot pair
plot.remarks: general remarks about the plot and whether the plot is edge or interior plot.
class: decay class of cwd. criteria for deciding decay classes is given in the supplementary (table s1)
state: whether the cwd is on the ground, is standing or is the remaining stump of a logged tree
dia1: 1st diameter of the cwd (cm)
dia2: 2nd diameter of the cwd (cm). this will be absent for standing cwd and stumps from past logging
cwd_group.pom: the point of measurement of the diameter, for standing cwd
height: height/length of the cwd (m)
cwd_group.hole: whether there was a cavity in the cwd
hole.depth: if there is a cavity, what is its depth (cm)
hole.dia: if there is a cavity, what is its diameter (cm)
cwd.remarks: general remarks about the cwd and shape of the cavity if present.
edg_int: whether the plot is an edge or interior plot.
treatment: whether its a plot near settlements (fuelwood_removal) or far away from settlements (control)

-----file 2: "nandakumar_et_al_cwd_density.csv"-----

description: this file contains the density of cwd of diameter greater than 10 cm in different decay classes. cwd were arbitrarily selected along different trails. cores were extracted from cwd from each density class and water displacement method was used for estimating density.

column names and description

place: site where the cwd was found
status: whether the cwd was fallen or standing. wether the cwd was fully touching the soil (on-ground) or starting to slant is indicated in square brackets
class: decay class of the cwd
code: unique code assigned to the cwd
volume 1-4: volume of the cores extracted from the cwd (cm3). if there were more than one core from a single cwd, they are assigned in different columns
mass: mass of the cores after air-drying till constant weight (g).
remarks.condition: remarks about the cwd and condition of the core.
dens: density of the core (g/m3), calculated using the formula volume/mass.

title: Socioecological dataset and cumulative threat index for Myristica swamp forests in Uttara Kannada, Western Ghats, India
codebook:
[README.txt]
README: Myristica Swamp Threat Assessment Dataset
Author: Priya Ranganathan

Overview:

This repository contains data and supporting materials for a socioecological assessment of Myristica swamp forests in Uttara Kannada, India. The study integrates ecological field data and community-derived information to assess ecosystem services, disservices, and site-level vulnerability.

Files included:

Swamp_Threat_Data.xlsx
Contains scored ecological and anthropogenic variables for 27 swamps, along with calculated weighted scores, cumulative threat index (CTI), and threat classification.
Variable_Definitions.xlsx
Provides detailed descriptions, scoring ranges, and weights for all variables included in the dataset.
Threat_Framework.pdf
Describes the scoring criteria, weighting rationale, and calculation of the cumulative threat index (CTI).
Interview_Guide_and_Questionnaire.pdf
Contains the structured survey instrument used to collect socioecological data, including ecosystem service perceptions, resource use, and cultural values.
Qualitative_Coding_Framework.pdf
Outlines the thematic coding scheme used to analyse open-ended interview responses, including ecosystem service categories, disservices, and knowledge classification criteria.

Survey instrument:

The questionnaire was used to assess local ecological knowledge, ecosystem service perceptions, and human–swamp interactions. It includes sections on:

Knowledge and interaction with swamps
Provisioning, regulating, supporting, and cultural ecosystem services
Perceived ecosystem disservices and human impacts
Demographic characteristics

Likert-scale questions (-2 to 2) were used to quantify perceived importance of ecosystem services, while open-ended responses were coded thematically using the provided coding framework.

The survey was administered in English and Kannada.

Methods summary:

Ecological and anthropogenic variables were scored using ordinal and binary scales reflecting levels of disturbance. Variables were weighted (1–3) based on their relative ecological impact.

A cumulative threat index (CTI) was calculated as a standardised weighted sum: CTI = Σ(Wᵢ × Sᵢ) / Σ(Wᵢ × Sᵢ,max)

Composite variables (e.g., resource use) were rescaled prior to analysis to ensure comparability. Swamps were classified into low, medium, and high threat categories based on terciles of the CTI distribution.

Qualitative data and coding

Open-ended interview responses were analysed using a deductive–inductive thematic coding approach. Themes were based on ecosystem service categories and emergent perceptions of disservices.

Respondents were also classified into knowledge categories (low/high) based on their interaction with and understanding of Myristica swamps.

Data limitations:

Raw interview transcripts and respondent-level data are not publicly available due to ethical and confidentiality considerations.

Swamp identifiers have been anonymised to protect sensit

title: Data from: Contrasting sap flow characteristics between pioneer and late-successional tree species in secondary tropical montane forests of Eastern Himalaya, India
codebook:
[README.txt]
# Sample_dataset_of_Sap_flow_Environment_for_FMBL_ManishKumar
---
The dataset contains 03 days of sample data from field research conducted at the Fambong-loh Wildlife sanctuary. Sap flux was measured using custom-built Granier's thermal dissipation probes. Microclimate observations were used to understand the drivers of stand transpiration. Air temperature (°C), relative humidity (Rh, %), wind speed (U, m s-1), and incoming short-wave radiation (Rs, kW m-2) were recorded using an automatic weather station (AWS) (Vantage-pro Davis Net, USA). On-site Precipitation (P, mm hr-1) was recorded using an automated tipping-bucket rain gauge. Hourly Vapour Pressure Deficit (D, kPa) was computed from air temperature and relative humidity. Soil water potential was recorded at 10 cm incremental depths from the topsoil to up to 30 cm depth using granular matrix-based (watermark) sensors (Virtual Electronics, Roorkee) and converted to volumetric water content using the site-specific van Genuchten water retention curve. Total soil moisture (S, mm hr-1) was computed for the topsoil (0-30 cm depth) using the trapezoidal method.
## Description of the data and file structure
Data consisting of 72 observations of 9 variables, including:
$ DATETIME: Time and date information in the format "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS"
 $ SOL : Incoming short-wave radiation (Rs, kW m-2), 
 $ VPD.final  : Vapour Pressure Deficit (VPD, kPa),
 $ TSM.mm     : Total Soil moisture (S, mm) 
$ WIND       : Wind speed in (u in m s-1 ) 
 $ vsf.KR     : Volumetric sap flow for Symplocos racemosa (VS. racemosa in kg h-1 ) 
 $ vsf.JH     : Volumetric sap flow for Eurya acuminata (VE.acuminata in kg h-1 )
 $ vsf.KT     : Volumetric sap flow for Castanopsis hystrix (VC.hystrix in kg h-1 )
Missing data is marked with NA.

## Sharing/Access information

##Links to other publicly accessible locations of the data:
  * NA

##Data was derived from the following sources:
  * Field data collection.


## Code/Software
The data analysis was done in R (version 4.2.3).

Abstract
Logging and hunting are two key direct threats to the survival of wildlife in the tropics, and also disrupt important ecosystem processes. We investigated the impacts of these two factors on the different stages of the seed dispersal cycle, including abundance of plants and their dispersers and dispersal of seeds and recruitment, in a tropical forest in north-east India. We focused on hornbills, which are important seed dispersers in these forests, and their food tree species. We compared abundances of hornbill food tree species in a site with high logging and hunting pressures (heavily disturbed) with a site that had no logging and relatively low levels of hunting (less disturbed) to understand logging impacts on hornbill food tree abundance. We compared hornbill abundances across these two sites. We, then, compared the scatter-dispersed seed arrival of five large-seeded tree species and the recruitment of four of those species. Abundances of hornbill food trees that are preferentially targeted by logging were two times higher in the less disturbed site as compared to the heavily disturbed site while that of hornbills was 22 times higher. The arrival of scatter-dispersed seeds was seven times higher in the less disturbed site. Abundances of recruits of two tree species were significantly higher in the less disturbed site. For another species, abundances of younger recruits were significantly lower while that of older recruits were higher in the heavily disturbed site. Our findings suggest that logging reduces food plant abundance for an important frugivore-seed disperser group, while hunting diminishes disperser abundances, with an associated reduction in seed arrival and altered recruitment of animal-dispersed tree species in the disturbed site. Based on our results, we present a conceptual model depicting the relationships and pathways between vertebrate-dispersed trees, their dispersers, and the impacts of hunting and logging on these pathways.

DATA & FILE OVERVIEW

1. Description of dataset

This data was generated from a study evaluating early survival and growth of native tree species, as part of the tropical forest restoration efforts in Arunachal Pradesh, Eastern Himalaya, India. 3022 saplings of 50 species were planted at a restorations site, out of which 17 species were examined for seasonal variation in survival and 9 species for seasonal variation in growth-rate (stem height and diameter).

2. Files

A. Descriptive files:

File 1: For an overall description of the data, see file: 
EcologicalRestoration_data_description.txt

File 2: 
For a description of the columns corresponding to the data, see file: 
EcologicalRestoration_schema.csv


B. Data files:

File 1: KM_test.csv (contains details of species that were measured for survival across three seasons- two wet and one dry season and the censoring status used for Kaplan Meier survival analysis)
File 2: GR.csv (contains details of the relative diameter and height growth-rates of nine tree species across three seasons- two wet and one dry)
File 3: RGR.csv (contains details of diameter and height of nine tree species measured across three seasons- two wet and one dry, used for the calculation of the relative diameter and height growth-rates)

C. R Code: 
RScript_EcologicalRestoration: is the RScript that was used for data analysis


METHODOLOGICAL INFORMATION

Growth-rate measurements- Negative readings for height were retained, whereas negative readings for stem diameter were converted to zero prior to the analysis.

This file describes the data in the accompanying five csv files in sequence. For the purpose of this data we define 'seed plot' as an experimental plot where seeds were laid out and their fates were monitored for a period of 50 days. Seed plot is sometimes referred as 'plot'. For more details regarding the methodology for data collection, please see the published paper.

A) 'Seed fate data.csv' file: Seeds of ten tree species were monitored and their fates were recorded at the end of monitoring period. Details regarding individual column names are as follows:

'tree_sp' represents the different tree species that were studied. The codes (and species names) are as follows: Ao (Actinodaphne obovata), Ba (Beilschmiedia assamica), Cc (Chisocheton cumingianus), Cr (Canarium resiniferum), Hk (Horsfieldia kingii), L1 (Litsea sp), Tp (Turpinia pomifera),Ea (Elaeocarpus aristatus), Pc (Prunus ceylanica), and Th (Talauma hodgsonii).

'location' refers to the location or placement of the plot and is noted as 'tree' when the plot was near a parent fruiting tree and 'random' when the plot was in a random location in the forest that was always over 50 m away from any parent tree. 

'plot_no.' is the serial number of the seed plots in different locations for each species. 

'total seeds' is the number of seeds that were placed in a plot at the beginning of an experiment.

'removed' is the number of seeds that were missing from a plot during the monitoring period. Such seeds were carried away from the plot by animals. 

'eaten' is the number of seeds that were preyed upon or eaten by animals visiting plots.

'alive' is the number of seeds that were alive or viable at the end of each experiment.

'dead' is the number of seeds that died due to fungal attack or insect infestation.

'germinated' includes seeds that germinated during the experiment period. 

B) 'Visitation rates.csv' file: This data was gathered using camera traps placed near seed plots to monitor the activity of animal visitors. The number of visits made by different animal species on seeds plots were recorded. Details regarding individual column names are as follows:

'tree_sp' means the different tree species that were studied. The codes (and species names) are as follows: Ao (Actinodaphne obovata), Ba (Beilschmiedia assamica), Cc (Chisocheton cumingianus), Cr (Canarium resiniferum), Hk (Horsfieldia kingii), Pc (Prunus ceylanica), and Th (Talauma hodgsonii).

'plot_no.' is the serial number of different plots for each tree species. 

'ct_nights' is the number of camera trap nights for which each plot was monitored.

'seeds' is the number of seeds placed inside each plot. 

'murid_visits' are the number of visits by murid rodents.

'porcupine_visits' are the number of visits by porcupines (Himalayan crestless porcupine and Brush-tailed porcupine).
'squirrel_visits' are the number of visits by the hoary-bellied squirrel.

This project contains data from a study investigating the gut passage times of five medium- and large-seeded tree species (Aglaia spectabilis, Beilschmiedia assamica, Polyalthia simiarum, Livistona jenkinsiana and Syzygium cumini) for three Asian Hornbills, the Oriental Pied Hornbill Anthracoceros albirostris, Rufous-necked Hornbill Aceros nipalensis and Wreathed Hornbill Rhyticeros undulatus in Nagaland Zoological Park, Dimapur. The trials were carried out on one male and one female each of the three species over multiple trials. Data was collected by Ms. Ushma Shukla, Ms. Akanksha Rathore, Dr. Rohit Naniwadekar and Dr. Aparajita Datta from Nature Conservation Foundation (www.ncf-india.org).

[readme_for_smj_shukla_etal_data_description.txt]
this project contains data from a study investigating the gut passage times of five medium- and large-seeded tree species (aglaia spectabilis, beilschmiedia assamica, polyalthia simiarum, livistona jenkinsiana and syzygium cumini) for three asian hornbills, the oriental pied hornbill anthracoceros albirostris, rufous-necked hornbill aceros nipalensis and wreathed hornbill rhyticeros undulatus  data was collected by ms. ushma shukla, ms. akanksha rathore, dr. rohit naniwadekar and dr. aparajita datta from nature conservation foundation (www.ncf-india.org). contactsrohit naniwadekar nature conservation foundation, amritha, 1311, 12th cross, vijayanagara 1st stage, mysore 570017, karnataka, india. email: rohit@ncf-india.org [corresponding author.]a brief description of the study is available on the ncf website:http://ncf-india.org/projects/tracking-hornbill-movements-and-seedsthe manuscript related to the study has been accepted in sarawak museum journal. abstractseed gut passage time through animals influence germination and displacement distance of seeds from parent plants. hornbills are the largest avian seed dispersers in asian tropical forests. in this study, we compared gut passage times for five large seeded tree species across gut passage trials, for three hornbill species. this study was conducted on six captive birds in nagaland, india. the gut passage time of seeds for the tree species varied from 5 to 536 minutes. there was no difference in gut passage times between trials, between male and female birds and different fruit tree species for the oriental pied hornbill. for the rufous-necked hornbill, we found differences in gut passage times across trials for beilschmiedia assamica and polyalthia simiarum, between individuals for livistona jenkinsiana and across tree species, especially for the female. for the wreathed hornbill, we found differences in gut passage times across trials for aglaia spectabilis and syzygium cumini, between individuals for beilschmiedia assamica and livistona jenkinsiana and across tree species only for the female bird. mean gut passage times reported here are higher than those reported previously for asian hornbills. context-specific variability in gut passage times highlights the need to examine the causes that result in these inconsistent patterns.

Besides this file (README.TXT), it contains the following comma-delimited text files with data in columns as explained below.

Tcode: Code used for transect in related publications: A to N in Raman et al. (2005), others in Raman and Sukumar 2002.
Type: Description of type of site
Refer: Indicated whether data from this transect was used in either of the two publications or both
LatitudeN: Approximate latitude in decimal degrees North of the midpoint of the transect
LongitudeE: Approximate longitude in decimal degrees East of the midpoint of the transect
AltimeterAvg: Average of altimeter readings (in metres above sea level) taken at 25 points spaced at 25 intervals along the transect 
LocationDetails: Description of location

2) 02_KMTRBIRD.csv: This file contains the data on birds from 5 minute variable radius point count surveys
TNo: Unique ID number or name of a 600 m long line transect
Date: Date of survey of the specified point
StTime: Start time of the point count
Pt: ID of the surveyed point along the 600 m long transect. Most transects started at A1 and had points marked every 25 m in 100 m chunks: A1...A4, B1...B4, ... upto F1...F4, after which it ended with X at the 600 m point. Alphabet codes may vary on longer trails and in some trails the numbers 1-25 were used to mark the points.  
Time: Specific time of observation
Spcode: Code used for bird species name
Species: English common name (India) of the bird species as used in the Ebird India portal in 2022.
No: Number of individuals detected
RD: Radial distance of the detected bird from the centre of the point in metres in the following radial distance classes: 0: 0-5 m; 5: 5-10 m, 10: 10-15 m, 15: 15-20 m; 20: 20-30 m; 30: 30-40 m; 40: 40-50 m; 50: >50 m)
HSF: Code indicating H = heard; S = seen; F = flying under the canopy (UC) or less than 5 m over the canopy (OC)
Remark: Notes and remarks (includes some codes: *: in mixed species flock; E: detected within the point sampling area while entering;  X: detected within point sampling area while leaving;  diff/DIFF/DF: different detection from conspecific; detected on the same point; GP: flock; CC: counter-calling individuals) 

3) 03_Birdnames.csv: This file contains bird species codes and matching commo

tcode: code used for transect in related publications: a to n in raman et al. (2005), others in raman and sukumar 2002.
type: description of type of site
refer: indicated whether data from this transect was used in either of the two publications or both
latituden: approximate latitude in decimal degrees north of the midpoint of the transect
longitudee: approximate longitude in decimal degrees east of the midpoint of the transect
altimeteravg: average of altimeter readings (in metres above sea level) taken at 25 points spaced at 25 intervals along the transect 
locationdetails: description of location

2) 02_kmtrbird.csv: this file contains the data on birds from 5 minute variable radius point count surveys
tno: unique id number or name of a 600 m long line transect
date: date of survey of the specified point
sttime: start time of the point count
pt: id of the surveyed point along the 600 m long transect. most transects started at a1 and had points marked every 25 m in 100 m chunks: a1...a4, b1...b4, ... upto f1...f4, after which it ended with x at the 600 m point. alphabet codes may vary on longer trails and in some trails the numbers 1-25 were used to mark the points.  
time: specific time of observation
spcode: code used for bird species name
species: english common name (india) of the bird species as used in the ebird india portal in 2022.
no: number of individuals detected
rd: radial distance of the detected bird from the centre of the point in metres in the following radial distance classes: 0: 0-5 m; 5: 5-10 m, 10: 10-15 m, 15: 15-20 m; 20: 20-30 m; 30: 30-40 m; 40: 40-50 m; 50: >50 m)
hsf: code indicating h = heard; s = seen; f = flying under the canopy (uc) or less than 5 m over the canopy (oc)
remark: notes and remarks (includes some codes: *: in mixed species flock; e: detected within the point sampling area while entering;  x: detected within point sampling area while leaving;  diff/diff/df: different detection from conspecific; detected on the same point; gp: flock; cc: counter-calling individuals) 

3) 03_birdnames.csv: this file contains bird species codes and matching commo

codebook:

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
				KERALA BIRD ATLAS DATASET - README
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
This folder consists of three input files (.RDS), one shape file (.shp) and one R script file (.R) for the analyses performed using the Kerala Bird Atlas: 2015-2020 dataset. 
These files are part of the publication "Kerala Bird Atlas 2015-2020: features, outcomes and implications of a citizen-science Project". There are no usage restrictions for this dataset except that all usages should provide an attribution as below

Kerala Bird Atlas Dataset (2021) Website Link. Accessed on DD Month Year

The outputs of this script are in the forms of shapefiles (.shp) and the attribute table contains the measured metrics.

This shapefile can be opened in QGIS/ArcGIS and the particular metric can be plotted.
In the script, only wet season data has been analyzed and the shapefiles have been generated. 
Dry season data can be analyzed by changing the word 'wet' to 'Dry' in the script and re-running the script.

The figures generated in the R platform were exported in svg format and annotated in Inkscape software.

The Cell IDs, Sub-cell IDs and List IDs of Great Hornbill (Buceros bicornis) records have not been provided since it is a sensitive species (https://ebird.org/india/news/ebird-sensitive-species). District names have been retained. Users interested in analyzing KBA records of Great Hornbill from any region (across Kerala or any district) may obtain the occurrence data from eBird by following due procedure for sensitive species (https://ebird.org/data/download/ebd), and get in touch with us for further assistance.

Contact:
Dr. P.O. Nameer, 
Professor (Wildlife), 
Kerala Agricultural University, Thrissur

codebook:
[README.txt]
﻿-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
				         README
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
This folder consists of four input files (.RDS) and one R script file (.R). These files are part of the publication "Functional diversity of the avian assemblages better than taxonomic diversity in capturing the effect of protection".
The figures generated in the R platform were exported in svg format and annotated in Inkscape software.

The description of four input files are as follows:

1.kba_data.rds: This file provides the raw dataset obtained as part of the Kerala Bird Atlas. This file contains following 9 columns-
"Common.Name" - Standard English names of the species detected during the Kerala Bird Atlas.
"Date" - Date of survey.
"Time" - Time of survey.
"n.observers" - Number of observers in the survey team.
"County" - District name.
"Sub.cell" - Unique code assigned to every surveyed sub-cell.
"Season" - Survey season; wet or dry.
"Cell.ID" - Unique code assigned to every surveyed cell.
"List.ID" - Unique checklist ID.
The geographic locations and List IDs of Great Hornbill (Buceros bicornis) records have not been provided since it is a sensitive species (https://ebird.org/india/news/ebird-sensitive-species). 

2.kba_names.rds: This file provides the list of species which were included in the analysis and taxa ('Spuhs','Slashes', Nocturnal and Pelagic species) which were eliminated from the raw dataset.
This file has following 4 columns-
"Common.Name"  - Standard English names of the species detected during the Kerala Bird Atlas.
"Scientific.Name" - Standard Binomial names of the species detected during the Kerala Bird Atlas.
"Action" - Suggests whether the species is to be reassigned a new name or is to be removed. e.g., 'Rock Pigeon' renamed to 'Rock Pigeon (Feral)'.    
"Assigned.Name.for.Atlas" - Provides the Standard English names or assigned names for all the species included in the analysis.

3.kba_species.details.rds: This file provides the details of 361 species detected during the Kerala Bird Atlas. Its 32 columns provides following information-
"Common.Name","Scientific.Name","Resident.status","IUCN.Redlist.Status","Distribution.Status","SoIB.status",
"Taxonomic order","Taxonomic Family","Endemicity","ForagingStrata","TrophicNiche","Diet.Inv","Diet.Vend",
"Diet.Vect","Diet.Vfish","Diet.Vunk","Diet.Scav","Diet.Fruit","Diet.Nect","Diet.Seed","Diet.PlantO",
"BodyMass.Value","Adult.survival","Maximum.longevity","Mean.clutch.size",
"Beak.Length","Beak.Width","Beak.Depth","Tarsus","Wing","HWI" (Hand-wing-index),"Tail"

#################################################################

Data from: Successional status, seed dispersal mode and overstorey species influence tree regeneration in tropical rain-forest fragments in Western Ghats, India
codebook:
[osuri_et_al_metadata.txt]
This dataset corresponds to the following publication:
Osuri, A. M., Chakravarthy, D., Mudappa, D., Raman, T. R. S., Ayyappan, N., Muthuramkumar, S., and Parthasarathy, N. 2017. Successional status, seed dispersal mode and overstorey species influence tree regeneration in tropical rain-forest fragments in Western Ghats, India. Journal of Tropical Ecology 33: 270-284. DOI: 10.1017/S0266467417000219

This is version 2 of the dataset with data provided in CSV format. Version 1 (http://datadryad.org/resource/doi:10.5061/dryad.vd0nn) contains the same data in .xlsx format.

The download includes a compressed folder that contains three CSV files whose contents are described below:
1) osuri_et_al_trees_regen_data.csv
2) osuri_et_al_trees_adult_data.csv
3) osuri_et_al_trees_traits_data.csv

-----File 1: "osuri_et_al_trees_regen_data.csv"-----
Description: The file contains records of all seedlings and saplings (1-5 cm diameter at breast height of 1.3 m, dbh) and larger trees (>5 cm dbh) recorded within 5m x 5m regeneration plots that were nested within 20m x 20m adult tree plots in two continuous forests and two forest fragments. Data were filtered during analysis to retain only seedling and saplings, defined as individuals with effective diameter <=5 cm.  

Column names and descriptions:
X: Row index
Site: Name of forest site
type: Habitat type, either "Cont" (continuous forest) or "Frag" (forest fragment)
P.No: An unique plot no. assigned to each 20m x 20m adult tree plot within each site
Q.no: An unique number assigned to each of four 10m x 10m quarters within each adult plot
nos: An unique number assigned to each individual seedling, sapling or tree within each site. 
old_code: Species codes used at the time of data collection (refer to traits data file for full species names)
species: Revised species codes consistent with current taxonomy
dbh, dbh.1 to dbh.34: Diameter at breast height of single- (dbh) and multi-stemmed (dbh - dbh.34) individuals, measured in centimetres (cm)    
eff.dbh: Effective diameter at breast height (cm)- calculated as ((dbh)^2 +(dbh.1)^2 +...+(dbh.34)^2)^(1/2), 
P.ID: Unique plot ID created by combining columns Site and P.No
-----

-----File 2: "osuri_et_al_trees_adult_data.csv"-----
Description: The file contains records of all adult trees >= 30 cm girth at breast height of 1.3 m (gbh) recorded within adult tree plots across two continuous forests and two forest fragments.

Column names and descriptions:

title: Data from: Local tropical forest restoration strategies affect tree recruitment more strongly than does landscape forest cover
codebook:
[Readme_-_Recruits_2015.txt]
Data Documentation for Islas Tree Recruits 2015

General Information
Name of data set: Tree recruits 2015

Name of data files in data set
Tree recruits 2015.csv

Date the data set was last modified: June 2016

Funder: National Science Foundation

How to cite data: Holl, K. D., J. L. Reid, J. M. Chaves-Fallas, F. Oviedo-Brenes & R. A. Zahawi. 2017. 
Local tropical forest restoration strategies affect tree recruitment more strongly than does landscape forest cover. 
Journal of Applied Ecology.

**

Methodology for data collection: For full details of experimental design and data collection see Holl et al. 2017.

In June-July 2015 (9-11 years after plot establishment), we sampled tree seedlings (>0.2 and <1 m tall) and saplings 
(>1 m tall and <5 cm d.b.h.) in all restoration and in reference forests at six sites remnant forest nearby that had 
not been logged or used for agriculture. We identified saplings in 40, 2  4 m quadrats in each plot (320 m2 per plot) 
and recorded seedlings in 1  2 m quadrats nested within the sapling quadrats (80 m2 total). Quadrats were distributed 
in four belt transects of 10 each in natural regeneration, plantation, and reference forest treatments with one randomly 
located in each of the four quadrants of the plot. In the applied nucleation treatment, quadrats where distributed along 
six belt transects aligned from the interior to outside the initial planted areas of the three nuclei sizes, with six adjacent 
quadrats in small and medium nuclei and seven in large nuclei. The 5-m edge at the perimeter of the plot was not sampled. 

Data collector(s): Karen Holl, Federico Oviedo-Brenes, Rakan Zahawi, J. Miguel Chaves-Fallas

Date of data collection: June-July 2015

Software (including version #) used to prepare data set: Microsoft Excel 2012.

Data processing that was performed: None

Person/people who entered data: Karen Holl and Andy Kulikowski 

Person/people who proofed data: Chad Oliver

Person to contact with questions: Karen Holl (kholl@ucsc.edu) 

Variables
Tree recruits 2015.csv
code: 6 letter code in most cases representing 3 letters of genus and 3 letters of species, see supplementary table in Holl et al. 2017 for full species names and families
site: Factor. Two-letter code denoting study site.
treat: Factor. One-letter code denoting restoration treatment: C=control (natural regeneration); I=island (applied nucleation); P=plantation; R=reference forest.
isl: Factor denoting island size. N=non-applicable; S=small (4 x 4 m); M=medium (8 x 8 m); L=large (12 x 12 m)
rep: Factor denoting permanent vegetation sampling location within plot. A=upper left quadrant, B=upper right quadrant, C=lower left quadrant, D=lower right quadrant.
SQ=2 x 4 m quadrat within a given replicate to note location. Quadrats were located sequentially numerically adjacent on the long edge.
abun: number of individuals per quadrat (2 m2 for seedlings and per 8 m2 for saplings)
szcl: size

isl: factor denoting island size. n=non-applicable; s=small (4 x 4 m); m=medium (8 x 8 m); l=large (12 x 12 m)
rep: factor denoting permanent vegetation sampling location within plot. a=upper left quadrant, b=upper right quadrant, c=lower left quadrant, d=lower right quadrant.
sq=2 x 4 m quadrat within a given replicate to note location. quadrats were located sequentially numerically adjacent on the long edge.
abun: number of individuals per quadrat (2 m2 for seedlings and per 8 m2 for saplings)
szcl: size

General Information
Name of data set: 
Effects of landscape structure on restoration success in tropical premontane forest
San-Jos et al. 2022

Name of data files in data set:
Landscape_variables.csv  landscape structure data measured in 17 radii surrounding 13 restoration sites with tree plantation treatment

Birds_database.csv  mean number of detections per year, over 7 years of highly forest dependent birds in 12 restoration sites with tree plantation treatment

Recruits_database.csv abundance (sum of new individuals) over 7 years of seedlings of late-successional species in 13 restoration sites with tree plantation treatment

Funder: 
National Science Foundation NSF-DEB 14-56520

How to cite data:
San Jos et al. (2022), Effects of landscape structure on restoration success in tropical premontane forest.  Scientific Reports 12: 13452


Data Collection
Description of data collected: Includes yearly surveys of tree recruitment (abundance of new individuals) and annual average detections of birds in tree plantations. 

Tree species successional stage was determined based on the expert opinion of two taxonomists who have each worked in the region for >20 years, herbarium specimens at Las Cruces, and literature resources (Chazdon et al. 2011 A novel statistical method for classifying habitat generalists and specialists. Ecology 92, 13321343. De Souza 2001 Seed size, seed germination, and seedling survival of Brazilian tropical tree species differing in successional status. Biotropica 33, 447457. Werden et al. 2020 Effects of dispersal- and niche-based factors on tree recruitment in tropical wet forest restoration. Ecol. Appl. 30, e02139). 

From all bird detections recorded, we extracted observations of species categorized as highly forest-dependent by BirdLife International (Buchanan et al. 2011 Identifying priority areas for conservation: a global assessment for forest-dependent birds. PLoS ONE 6, e29080)

Full data-collection methodology can be found in:  

Reid, J. L., Mendenhall, C. D., Rosales, J. A., Zahawi, R. A. & Holl, K. D. Landscape context mediates avian habitat choice in tropical forest restoration. PLoS ONE 9, e90573 (2014).

Holl, K. D., Reid, J. L., Chaves-Fallas, J. M., Oviedo-Brenes, F. & Zahawi, R. A. Local tropical forest restoration strategies affect tree recruitment more strongly than does landscape forest cover. J. Appl. Ecol. 54, 10911099 (2017).

Date of data collection: Tree recruitment data collected annually in June-July from 2011-2017. Bird data collected three times per year from 2011-2017. Landscape structure data measured from aerial images from 2014.

title: Data from: Plant-disperser mutualisms in a semi-arid habitat invaded by Lantana camara L.

[READ ME.txt]
************************READ ME***********************************************************************************

This is a folder containing data and code for the statistical analysis and figures presented in the paper " Plant-disperser mutualisms in a semi-arid habitat invaded by Lantana camara L.".

This folder contains a copy of the main data files exactly as used for this paper, as well as a script file to run statistical analyses and the generate the figures in this paper. 

Plant nomenclature follows: Gamble, J.S. 1923. Flora of the Presidency of Madras. Adlard & Son, London, UK. and was cross-checked/updated with www.plantlist.org. 
Bird nomenclature follows: Grimmett, R., Inskipp, C. & Inskipp, T. 1999. Pocket Guide to the Birds of the Indian Subcontinent. Oxford University Press,  Chicago. 


********************************Contents**************************************************************************
There are 4 files in this folder:

1. README.txt: This file, contains a description of all data files and script files used for this paper. 

2. SMdata.csv: A .csv file containing measurements of fruit and seed morphology of 10 fleshy-fruited, bird-dispersed shrub species from a semi-arid habitat. Missing data are indicated by "NA". Some of these data are summarised in Table 1 of the paper. 

3. TWdata.csv: a .csv file containing tree-watch (scan and focal) behavioural observations on birds visiting and feeding at 15 individuals of 10 shrub species. "NA" in this file does *not* represent missing data. During scan observation, only frugivore identity and their numbers are noted while their behaviour is not. "NA", thus represents 'not observed'. Some of these data are summarised in Table 2 of the paper

4. Dispersal mutualism invaded network.R : an R file with the code for statistical analyses and graphical presentation of results. 
A data frame called "Frug.data" created within this file contains data compiled from the 2 input files. Statistical model summaries have been compled in Table 3 of the paper. The script file draws Fig 1 of the paper with short, 4-letter codes for plant and bird names (see below). The codes have been expanded to the taxonomic names in the figures submitted to the journal. The expansions were made externally on Microsoft Power Point.

this project contains data from a study carried out around wildlife insititute of india (wii) campus in dehradun, in the western-himalayan region, india. 
the data was collected by ms. yukti v.taneja for master's dissertation study under the guidance of dr. navendu page and r. suresh kumar of wii and dr. rohit naniwadekar of nature conservation foundation (ncf, india) 

contacts
yukti v. taneja 
email: yuktitaneja.20@gmail.com [corresponding author]

the manuscript related to the study has been accepted in forest ecology and management. the title of the manuscript is "effects of canopy cover on fruiting intensity and fruit removal of a tropical invasive weed".
the authors of the manuscript are yukti v.taneja, navendu v. page, r. suresh kumar and rohit naniwadekar. 

abstract
lantana camara (hereafter, lantana) is among the worst invasive alien plants spread extensively across africa, australia and asia at an alarming rate, posing significant challenges to conservation of native biodiversity. while, lantana invasion is widely recognised to be more pronounced in open-canopy habitats (including deciduous forests, forest edges and gaps), the potential role of variation in seed dispersal across habitats varying in overstory canopy cover is poorly understood. avian frugivores are among primary seed dispersers of the fleshy-fruited lantana. we monitored 45 lantana shrubs across a gradient of overstory canopy cover to determine the relationship between fruiting intensity and canopy cover. we watched 80 lantana shrubs (240 h) across a canopy cover gradient to determine 1) differences in frugivore assemblage visiting lantana across open- and closed-canopy habitats, 2) drivers of frugivore visitation on lantana, and 3) relationship between seed disperser visitation rate and overstory canopy cover. we found that lantana shrubs under low overstory canopy cover had higher fruit abundance than those in high canopy cover. frugivore assemblage differed between lantana shrubs in open- versus closed-canopy cover habitats. drivers of frugivore visitation on lantana varied across different frugivore species with a greater probability of occurrence of bulbuls (the primary seed dispersers of lantana) on shrubs under low overstory canopy cover. visitation rates of the effective seed dispersers were higher on shrubs under low overstory canopy cover. thus, there was greater chances of dispersal of seeds in habitats with low overstory canopy cover. the study demonstrates variable fruiting intensity and fruit removal rate as a driver of differences in dispersal of seeds across habitats. it highlights greater vulnerability of open habitats to invasion and the need to prioritise lantana management efforts in open habitats. anthropogenic activities that lead to "b504c6c1-f7cf-4811-bff1-f382274b7011","123456789/139","NA","Vardien, Waafeka","2012-03-01T06:28:04Z","2012-03-01T06:28:04Z","2010-2012","2012-03-01T06:28:04Z","The overall objective of my M.Sc project was to improve the current knowledge of the invasion dynamics of an invasive plant species, Lantana camara L., in South Africa’s flagship protected area, Kruger National Park (KNP). Lantana camara is a global invader, occurring in approximately 60 countries and islands. The species is able to spread rapidly into regions where it has been introduced and is associated with a variety of negative impacts. Attempts at biological control of the species has had limited success owing to its uncertain taxonomy, ease of hybridisation and broad ecological amplitude. 

An understanding of how L. camara establishes, spreads and disperses within protected areas will aid management efficiency, for example, by prioritizing areas for management operations. This thesis specifically explores the history, mechanisms of invasion, distribution patterns and spatial extent of dispersal of L. camara. The latter was restricted to a landscape scale, using in a river catchment system in the KNP as model system. 

The thesis consists of three chapters. The first two are research chapters and the third a brief conclusion. In chapter one of the thesis I reviewed L. camara invasions in South Africa, with particular reference to the known drivers of invasive success. Specifically, the processes and factors that have contributed to the successful invasion of the species are explained using a framework developed for invasion ecology. Distribution patterns across biomes, ecoregions, and under current and changing climate scenarios

codebook:
[00_README.txt]
TITLE

Tree and habitat structure data from rainforest fragments and coffee plantations in the Anamalai Hills, Western Ghats, India 

DESCRIPTION

This dataset contains point-centred quarter (PCQ) data on trees and habitat structure measurements data from rainforest fragments and some coffee plantations in the Valparai Plateau and Anamalai Tiger Reserve, Tamil Nadu, India. The data were gathered to quantity habitat parameters for bird and small carnivorous mamm community studies. Data were gathered mainly by T. R. Shankar Raman and Divya Mudappa (2000 to 2003), Hari Sridhar (2005), and Akshay Surendra (2019). 

Publications

Specific portions of the dataset have been used in the following publications:

Mudappa, D. 2001. Ecology of the brown palm civet Paradoxurus jerdoni in the tropical rainforests of the Western Ghats, India. Ph. D. thesis, Bharathiar University, Coimbatore. https://hdl.handle.net/10603/101890

Raman, T. R. S. 2001. Community ecology and conservation of mid-elevation tropical rainforest bird communities in the southern Western Ghats, India. PhD thesis, Indian Institute of Science, Bangalore. https://archive.org/details/raman-2001-ph-d-thesis-iisc

Raman, T.R.S. 2006. Effects of Habitat Structure and Adjacent Habitats on Birds in Tropical Rainforest Fragments and Shaded Plantations in the Western Ghats, India. Biodiversity and Conservation 15: 1577–1607. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10531-005-2352-5

Sridhar, H., & Sankar, K. 2008. Effects of habitat degradation on mixed-species bird flocks in Indian rain forests. Journal of Tropical Ecology 24: 135-147. doi:10.1017/S0266467408004823

Surendra, A. & Raman, T. R. S. 2022. Forest bird decline and community change over 19 years in long-isolated South Asian tropical rainforest fragments. Preprint. BioRxiv 2022.10.22.513365; doi: https://doi.org/10.1101/2022.10.22.513365 

A related dataset is the following:
Raman, T. R. S. (2020). Data from: Effects of Habitat Structure and Adjacent Habitats on Birds in Tropical Rainforest Fragments and Shaded Plantations in the Western Ghats, India [Dataset]. Dryad. https://doi.org/10.5061/dryad.4mw6m907q

Curation and corrections
Data were collated, curated, and corrected before this upload. Besides addition of new columns, explanations of metadata, and other corrections included few related to canopy measurements, effective girth of multi-stem trees, and species identification.

We are grateful to P. Jeganathan and P. R. Shankar for assistance with data collection in 2000. Others who assisted with field research, and funding agencies related to the specific studies, are acknowledged in the above publications.

title: Data from: Mammal persistence and abundance in tropical rainforest remnants in the southern Western Ghats, India
codebook:
[00_README.txt]
This dataset contains data from the following publication: 
Sridhar, H., Raman, T. R. S. & Mudappa, D. 2008. Mammal persistence and abundance in tropical rainforest remnants in the southern Western Ghats, India. Current Science 94: 748-757. 
URL: https://www.currentscience.ac.in/Volumes/94/06/0748.pdf
URL2: https://www.jstor.org/stable/24100628
Corrigendum:
Sridhar, H., Raman, T. R. S. & Mudappa, D. 2009. Corrigendum: mammal persistence and abundance in tropical rainforest remnants in the southern Western Ghats, India. Current Science 97: 612-613.
URL: https://www.currentscience.ac.in/Volumes/97/05/0612.pdf

Description of dataset:
The data contains detections of mammals and hornbills (and few incidental records of other species) made along line transect surveys and opportunistic surveys in the Valparai Plateau and Anamalai Tiger Reserve, Tamil Nadu, India. Further details of the Study Area and methods are available in Sridhar et al. (2008), but methods are briefly described below. 
Five rainforest patches were chosen within IGWLS and four privately-owned rainforest fragments in the Valparai plateau. Fifteen line transects, ranging in length from 1 to 3 km were laid across the nine sites, with the three largest sites having 2–4 transects each. The total distance covered by all transects was 32.02 km. Each transect was walked five times between September 2005 and April 2006 following standard distance sampling protocol. Two observers walked each transect at 0.75–1 km/h. For each detection, we recorded species, group size and perpendicular distance (measured using a rangefinder) from the transect. For animals which occurred in groups, perpendicular distances were measured to group centres. Apart from detections on transects, attempts were made to obtain group sizes of mammal species whenever incidentally detected. All transects were walked between 0630 and 1000 h. Indirect evidence (scat, tracks) on transects and incidental sightings (direct and indirect) of mammals were also recorded.

Columns in the data file (Anamalai_plant_invasion_data.csv)

LAT: Latitude in decimal degrees (N) recorded on Garmin etrex GPS unit with WGS 84 Datum
LONG: Longitude in decimal degrees (E) recorded on Garmin etrex GPS unit with WGS 84 Datum
FRAGMENT: Forest fragment areas surveyed in study with the following 6 acronyms corresponding to 4 sites:
    TF: Tata Finlay fragment
    PA: Pannimade fragment
    PA(DE): Disturbed portion of PA fragment with Eucalyptus plantation 
    PA(EVE): Relatively undisturbed portion of PA fragment with evergreen forest
    PU: Puthuthottam fragment
    MB: Manamboli fragment
SITE: The 4 forest fragments where data were collected = TF, PA, PU, and MB Fragments
TRANSECTNO: Replicate transects laid from edge into interior of each study site, named as A, B, C, D, E, F, G
QUADRATNO: Replicate 10 m x 10 m quadrat laid along each transect. A maximum of 12 quadrats (100 sq m) were laid and numbered from 1 (closest to coffee plantation edge) to 12 (interior of fragment)
COFDIST: Distance in metres from coffee plantation edge to nearest edge of quadrat
CDISTCENTRE: Distance in metres from coffee plantation edge to centre of quadrat
FRAGEDGEDIST: Distance in metres from fragment edge to nearest edge of quadrat
FDISTCENTRE: Distance in metres from fragment edge to centre of quadrat

CANOVE: Canopy overlap estimated from the centre of the quadrat with ranks: 0-no tree canopy overhead, 1-tree canopies present but not touching each other, 2-tree canopies overlapping with sky visible through leaves, 3-tree canopies overlapping and sky not visible through leaves.

columns in the data file (anamalai_plant_invasion_data.csv)
sno: serial number
date: date in a month/date/year format
time: indian standard time (standard time + 0530 utc)
wpno: waypoint number recorded on gps (geographical positioning system) unit (garmin, etrex) using wgs84 datum
lat: latitude in decimal degrees (n) recorded on garmin etrex gps unit with wgs 84 datum
long: longitude in decimal degrees (e) recorded on garmin etrex gps unit with wgs 84 datum
fragment: forest fragment areas surveyed in study with the following 6 acronyms corresponding to 4 sites:
    tf: tata finlay fragment
    pa: pannimade fragment
    pa(de): disturbed portion of pa fragment with eucalyptus plantation 
    pa(eve): relatively undisturbed portion of pa fragment with evergreen forest
    pu: puthuthottam fragment
    mb: manamboli fragment
site: the 4 forest fragments where data were collected = tf, pa, pu, and mb fragments
transectno: replicate transects laid from edge into interior of each study site, named as a, b, c, d, e, f, g
quadratno: replicate 10 m x 10 m quadrat laid along each transect. a maximum of 12 quadrats (100 sq m) were laid and numbered from 1 (closest to coffee plantation edge) to 12 (interior of fragment)
cofdist: distance in metres from coffee plantation edge to nearest edge of quadrat
cdistcentre: distance in metres from coffee plantation edge to centre of quadrat
fragedgedist: distance in metres from fragment edge to nearest edge of quadrat
fdistcentre: distance in metres from fragment edge to centre of quadrat
slope: slope of the terrain where quadrat was located, visually ranked as 0-flat (o to 5 degrees), 1-gentle (5-20 degrees), 2-medium (20-45 degrees), 3-steep (above 45 deg)
traildist: distance to nearest human foot trail in metres from the edge of quadrat; if trail was present within a quadrat then distance was recorded as 0 m 
othedge: distance in metres from other edge of the fragment (opposite to fragment edge with coffee plantation)
cancov: canopy cover estimated as percentage of closed canopy directly above the centre of the quadrat using spherical densiometer
canove: canopy overlap estimated from the centre of the quadrat with ranks: 0-no tree canopy overhead, 1-tree canopies present but not touching each other, 2-tree canopies overlapping with sky visible through leaves, 3-tree canopies overlapping and sky not visible through leaves.

abstract: this dataset contains abundance data on large carnivores and their prey species, using direct and indirect sign surveys along line and belt transects, respectively, as well as data on remains of prey species in large carnivore scats. this dataset is part of a study (published paper under related works) on leopard ecology in a landscape containing commercial plantations of tea and coffee, and rainforest fragments and protected area. these data were collected between 2008 and 2010 in valparai plateau and anamalai tiger reserve in the western ghats, india. the dataset contains following files:

1) transect_details.csv 
2) transect_repeats.csv
3) mammals_direct_signs.csv
4) mammals_indirect_signs.csv
5) large_carnivores_indirect_signs.csv
6) large_carnivore_diet.csv

more details regarding the above files can be found in readme_data_columnnames.txt.

options fields
..............
keyword(s):

leopards, panthera, pardus, large carnivore diet, prey abundance, plantation, tropical rainforest 

methods: 

sign surveys: direct surveys for mammal were conducted using line transects (2-km-long) and indirect sign surveys using belt transects (2 km long and 2 m wide) in four different habitat types: continuous forest as control site, coffee plantation, forest fragment, and tea plantation.

diet analysis: scats were analysed for predator diet using indigestible remains of prey species, particularly hairs, bones, quills and feathers. hairs were identified based on external morphology, cuticular and medullary patterns, and ratio of medulla to cortex in cross-section, with the help of a microscope and comparing with photographs of reference slides.

please see the paper (under related works) for more details on methods.

committee of the iucn, tropical rainforest programme.

project title: baseline assessment of vegetation status for ecological restoration of discontinued plantations and degraded forests in the manar estate, nilgiris

project overview

this dataset and the associated project report (gamuz a.s. 2024, nature conservation foundation) are part of a long-term forest and grassland  restoration project in the manar estate, craigmore plantations, kolacamby, in the southern nilgiris, western ghats, india. the targeted area for restoration has been divided into 100 grids of 1 ha (100x100 metre) each, of which vegetation within 70 accessible grids were surveyed; the remaining 30 grids were either too steep, or chockablock with native thorny bushes that could neither be cleared nor measured.

the vegetation survey primarily comprised of (1) trees identified and measured for girth and height within 20x20 m plots located at the centroid of each grid (manar_vegetation_survey_trees.csv), and (2) saplings and seedlings identified and enumerated within 5x5 m plots at the centre of each 20x20m plot (manar_vegetation_survey_saplings_seedlings.csv).

in addition, this dataset includes (3) the species identity of large trees with canopies that overtopped in the manar estate5x5 m plots from outside the circumscribing 20x20 m plot (manar_vegetation_survey_overheadtrees_additional.csv), and (4) ocular estimates of vegetation (and other) cover scored on a tertile scale for each accessible grid (manar_vegetation_survey_cover.csv)

codebook:
[README.txt]
All data present here correspond to the coexistence experiment described in Weatherby et al. (1998), Journal of Animal Ecology, 67, 554–566, and re-used in de Goër de Herve et al. (2023)


The original data are presented as four pdf files are here, scanned from A. Weatherby's thesis (which exists only as a printed version ; original numeric data files were lost). In addition, two csv tables correspond to recent transcriptions performed by M. de Goër de Herve in order to analyze them numerically.

Only the "presence-absence.csv" was used for the data analysis presented in this repository, the other tables are presented for completeness (final_results-summary is a summary of presence-absence which is itself a summary of abundance_data).

-------------------------------

1a. presence-absence.pdf - This table summarizes which species are present or absent at each census, for each replicate. An "X" indicates that the replicate was discontinued. Black lines correspond to failed replicates.

1b. presence-absence.csv - Hand transcription of the previous file, with a couple typo corrections (removing a doubled X at the end of experiment 27:6, adding Xs at the end of experiments 29:4 and 49:3).


---------------------------------

2a. abundance_data.pdf - This is a table of the results for all replicates, for all scans, including the abundance estimates (using the 5 point scale described in the Methods section of A. Weatherby's thesis - see document 4 "abundance-methods.pdf").

As indicated in the key at the top a dash indicates a species not being recorded (i.e. believed to be absent), an "X" indicates when a replicate was discontinued. Numbers, including "0", indicate a species present and its estimated logarithmic abundance class, with a zero indicating a species present but at very low density, rather than a species absence.

At the right hand end of the table there are some additional columns.  In general these indicate (in order L to R): (i) the state reached which satisfied one of the stopping criteria, (ii) the scan at which that occurred, (iii) the date of that scan, (iv, v, vi) the last three columns are similar information for cases where (for various reasons) microcosms were run on past that point - for our purposes here these can be ignored I think. 

None of these summary columns are necessary, as all the information is contained in the table itself.  Additionally, in a few cases there are minor differences in the list of states in the 'CRITERIA' column from those in the paper and summary. The reason for this is that in a few cases (as explained in the paper) microcosms had not satisfied the stopping criteria by scan 4, but as these were rather few, we settled on using the states at scan 4 as the endpoints in all microcosms for the analysis in the paper. Of course, the information here would allow a different approach to be taken if required. The basic message is, however, do not take the states in the "CRITERIA" as being strictly equivalent 
[README.txt]
Here are the source data files used for the model-data comparison presented in the article. The experimental data are present in the presence-absence.csv file, while the computed model outputs are split into a node and edges files.

== Description of data files ==

1. presence-absence.csv - experimental data, copied from the data folder

-----------------------------

2. nodes.csv - contains the list of all nodes (sets of species) in the computed transition network (see Gaucherel & Pommereau 2019).

- "node" corresponds to the node identifier
- "succ" to its successors allowed by rules
- "pred" to its possible predecessors
- "on" to the species which are present in the node
- "off" to the species which are present in the node
- "dead" is "VRAI" (True) when the state is a deadlock, and "FAUX" (False) otherwise
- "transient" is irrelevant here
- "component" corresponds to the identifier of the graph component (set of nodes which share the same possible outcome)
